Fur- ther placebo-controlled studies have shown an increased risk of mortality with the use of the atypical antipsychotics aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine, and risperidone in these patients; most of the deaths appeared due to cardio- vascular events or infection. Consequently, in 2005 the FDA issued advice against the use of all atypicals, includ- ing clozapine and ziprasidone in patients with dementia- related psychosis20 (for further details, see Dementia, un- der Risperidone, p.1024). Furthermore, a large multicentre study21 concluded that adverse effects of atypical antipsy- chotics (olanzapine, quetiapine, and risperidone) outweigh their benefits in treating behavioural disturbances in pa- tients with Alzheimer’s disease. A long-term placebo-con- trolled study22 in patients with Alzheimer’s disease given antipsychotics (chlorpromazine, haloperidol, risperidone, thioridazine, or trifluoperazine) also concluded that, for most patients, stopping antipsychotic therapy had no over- all detrimental effect on functional and cognitive status. The authors suggested that although antipsychotics may have some value in the maintenance treatment of more se- vere behavioural disturbances, any potential benefits must be weighed against the risk of serious adverse effects. In addition, in 2008, the FDA extended its advice against the use of antipsychotics in elderly patients with dementia-re- lated psychosis to include classical antipsychotics;23 the FDA were aware of 2 observational studies showing that the risk of death in such patients taking classical antipsy- chotics was similar to that seen in those taking atypical an- tipsychotics. Methodological limitations precluded any conclusion that classical antipsychotics have a greater mortality risk than atypical antipsychotics. The sedative drug, clomethiazole, may be a useful alterna- tive to antipsychotics for the control of agitated behaviour in elderly patients, generally causing fewer adverse ef- fects; respiratory depression, excessive sedation, and de- pendence may, however, be a problem. Benzodiazepines are not generally indicated for the management of elderly demented patients because of the risks of dependence with continued use, disinhibiting effects, and the particular problems of these drugs in old people (see the Elderly, un- der Diazepam, p.989).
